result: GCaMP6 reporter mice (Ai95, Ai96, Ai93) crossed with Emx1-IRES-Cre were used for fluorescence imaging through a 5 mm cranial window, with all three lines showing significantly greater baseline fluorescence than wild-type mice.
evaluation: Claims C2, C14, C20-C27 describe the experimental setup and baseline fluorescence measurements. The quantitative data (C25-C27) showing 10.3±1.3, 4.7±0.5, and 49.7±5.9 fold increases over wild-type are specific and supported by Figure 1H. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate controls.

result: All three GCaMP6 mouse lines displayed larger amplitude and faster kinetics of fluorescence changes compared to wild-type autofluorescence, with Emx1-Ai93 showing the largest response (10±2.4% ΔF/F, 216× wild-type) and fastest kinetics (219±60 ms latency to peak).
evaluation: Claims C28-C47 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of GCaMP6 responses across three mouse lines with appropriate wild-type controls. The data show consistent patterns with detailed kinetic measurements (latency, rise time, decay time) for each line. Statistical measures (mean±SEM, ranges, sample sizes) are provided throughout.

result: Retinotopic maps were generated using a spherically-corrected drifting checkerboard stimulus (0.043-0.048 Hz) in awake, head-restrained mice, with 10-40 stimulus presentations averaged per direction and automated border identification using a manually-tuned threshold (mean 0.32±0.004).
evaluation: Claims C48-C59 describe the retinotopic mapping methodology with appropriate detail. The stimulus parameters, averaging procedures, and analysis pipeline are clearly specified. The threshold robustness analysis (C57, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) demonstrates that results are stable across the parameter range employed (0.2-0.4).

result: Eye movements during mapping were characterized (up to 5-10° vertical, 15-20° horizontal), but with mean displacement <1° and movements occurring during all stimulus phases, the effects were eliminated by averaging. A constant mean luminance stimulus was used to minimize pupil size changes.
evaluation: Claims C60-C65 address a critical potential confound with appropriate measurements and controls. The eye tracking data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) support the conclusion that averaging eliminates movement artifacts. The constant luminance design (C64) and pupil measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) provide additional validation.

result: Most field sign patches were visible after only 15 minutes of imaging (10 sweeps per direction), maps were stable across imaging sessions, and displayed consistent structure across mice, representing a practical advantage over prior reflectance-based methods requiring 1-2 hours.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 demonstrate the efficiency and reproducibility of the GCaMP6 method. The 15-minute mapping time (C71) is supported by Figure 3A, stability across sessions is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 (C72), and the comparison to prior methods (C73) is appropriately cited to Garrett et al. 2014.

result: GCaMP6 fluorescence mapping revealed three new field sign patches: MMA and MMP (medial to AM and PM in the MM region) appeared consistently across mice (>85% incidence, significant k-means clusters), while RLL (anterior-lateral to RL) was less consistent (60% incidence, non-significant cluster).
evaluation: Claims C3, C16, C76, C80-C81, C83-C84, C107, C111-C112, C116 describe the identification of new retinotopic patches. The consistency of MMA and MMP is supported by multiple metrics: appearance in mean field sign map (C84), high incidence (C94, C111), and significant k-means clustering (C109, C111). RLL shows lower consistency (C106, C110, C112) but still appears in the mean map.

result: Across 14 mice (4 Emx1-Ai96, 10 Emx1-Ai93), the maximum number of field sign patches in individual maps was 9 positive and 7 negative, with 10 patches (V1, LM, LI, AL, RL, AM, PM, MMA, MMP, P) occurring in >85% of mice.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89, C94 provide quantitative summary of mapping results across mice. The data show consistency between mouse lines (C87-C89) and identify highly reproducible patches (C94). Sample sizes are appropriate (14 mice total) and the quantitative metrics are clearly stated.

result: The ability to map additional regions of retinotopic organization likely results from the superior signal-to-noise ratio of GCaMP6, as the newly identified patches (MMA, MMP, RLL, LLA) showed smaller fluorescence changes than established visual areas, with RLL showing the weakest activation.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114, C117-C118 provide a mechanistic explanation for the discovery of new patches. The hypothesis (C113) is supported by quantitative data showing smaller amplitude responses in the new patches (C114, Figure 3F), with RLL showing the smallest changes (C117), consistent with its lower mapping consistency (C118).

result: The newly identified field sign patches extend >2 mm beyond V1 borders, likely extending into architectonically-defined retrosplenial cortex (medial extension of PM) and barrel cortex (RLL and possibly RL), based on anatomical constraints.
evaluation: Claims C119-C125 make anatomical inferences about the location of new patches. The >2 mm extent (C119) is a quantitative observation. The inferences about retrosplenial (C122-C123) and barrel cortex (C124-C125) are reasonable based on known anatomical boundaries, though these remain inferences pending direct confirmation.

result: Comparison of retinotopic maps to chemoarchitectonic borders (cytochrome oxidase staining, 4 Emx1-Ai96 mice) confirmed that retinotopic organization extends into primary somatosensory cortex (with RLL mapping to posterior barrels B and C) and retrosplenial cortex, with a mismatch of 312±88 μm between chemoarchitectonic and functional V1 borders.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C126-C130, C155-C156 describe a major finding using careful registration methods (fluorescent vasculature labeling, Figure 4). The extension into barrel cortex is directly demonstrated (C127-C128), and the border mismatch is quantified (C130). The registration approach addresses potential alignment artifacts (C132).

result: Using Rorb-Ai93 mice where cytoarchitectonic borders are inherently aligned with functional maps (eliminating tissue processing artifacts), the lateral V1 border mismatch was confirmed at 120±38 μm (10 mice), with the cytoarchitectonic border running through functionally-defined RL and LM.
evaluation: Claims C133-C139 provide independent confirmation of the border mismatch using a different approach that eliminates potential registration artifacts (C137). The Rorb expression pattern (C134, cited to Allen Brain Atlas) provides the basis for this method. The mismatch magnitude (139 μm, C139) is smaller than with CO staining but in the same direction.

result: In Emx1-Ai93 mice, cytoarchitectonic borders were visible after averaging resting GCaMP6 fluorescence from 10 mice, showing a V1 border mismatch of 236 μm, consistent with the Rorb-Ai93 and cytochrome oxidase results.
evaluation: Claims C140-C143 provide a third independent measurement of the border mismatch using averaged Emx1-Ai93 fluorescence. The mismatch magnitude (236 μm, C143) is intermediate between the CO staining (312 μm) and Rorb-Ai93 (120 μm) measurements, supporting the consistency of this finding across methods.

result: Analysis of projection-based retinotopy from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (99 mice with V1 injections, registered to a 3D reference atlas from 1675 mice) showed that the myeloarchitectonic V1 border was 180 μm lateral to the projection-based retinotopic border, and that LLA extends into auditory cortex.
evaluation: Claims C145-C154 provide a fourth independent assessment of the border mismatch using a large dataset and different methodology (projection-based retinotopy). The 180 μm mismatch (C154) is consistent with the other three measurements (mean 212 μm across all four methods, C160). The extension of LLA into auditory cortex (C152) is an additional finding.

result: There is a consistent mismatch between architectonic and retinotopic V1 borders across three methods (chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic, myeloarchitectonic), with the architectonic border lateral to the retinotopic border by up to ~300 μm (mean 212 μm across four measurements: 312, 120, 236, 180 μm).
evaluation: Claims C159-C160 synthesize the border mismatch findings across all four measurement approaches. The consistency across methods (chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic in two mouse lines, and myeloarchitectonic) strongly supports this as a real phenomenon rather than a methodological artifact. The quantitative summary (mean 212 μm) is appropriate.

result: 2-photon imaging of layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron receptive fields (964 neurons, 3 experiments) at the V1-LM border showed that single-cell retinotopy reversed at the widefield-defined border, with the single-cell border only 30 μm lateral of the widefield border—insufficient to account for the 100-300 μm architectonic-retinotopic mismatch.
evaluation: Claims C161-C173 provide critical validation that widefield and single-cell borders align closely (30 μm difference, C172), ruling out population averaging as an explanation for the architectonic mismatch (C173). The sample size (964 neurons) is substantial, and the orderly retinotopic progression (C167, C170-C171) with reversal at the widefield border (C168) strongly supports the widefield measurements.

result: GCaMP6 fluorescence-based maps differ from previous maps in that area P extends across the posterior border of V1 from LM to PM, and area M is displaced medially relative to Garrett et al. (2014), resulting in an almost continuous ring of positive field sign areas surrounding V1, broken only by AM.
evaluation: Claims C174-C176 describe differences from prior maps with appropriate citation (C175). The extension of P (C174) and medial displacement of M (C175) are clearly shown in the figures. The resulting ring organization (C176) is a notable organizational feature, though the functional significance requires further investigation.

result: The four positive field sign patches bordering V1 (LM, RL, PM, P) display complementary representations biased toward different visual field quadrants (LM: upper nasal; RL: lower nasal; P: upper temporal; PM: lower temporal), with summed coverage approximating V1 and overlap primarily at the central hemifield (7.4±2.1° altitude, 37.8±1.4° azimuth).
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C177-C185 describe the visual field coverage analysis. The complementary organization with quadrant biases (C178-C182) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 8. The quantitative center of coverage (C184) and overlap pattern (C183, C185) are well-supported by the data. This represents a comprehensive characterization of visual field representation.

result: The arrangement of four positive field sign areas (RL, LM, P, PM) forming an almost continuous ring around V1 (broken only by AM) resembles the primate visual system where V1 is surrounded by V2, though mouse V2 was historically split into multiple areas (LM, RL, etc.) due to overlapping maps.
evaluation: Claims C186-C189 make an interesting comparative observation with appropriate citations to primate studies (C186) and the history of mouse visual area nomenclature (C187-C188). The complementary visual field representations (C189) support this organizational similarity, though functional homology would require additional evidence.

result: The measured visual field coverage (V1: ~60° altitude, ~90° azimuth) likely underestimates true coverage compared to single-cell recordings (~100° altitude, ~150° azimuth) because widefield mapping emphasizes receptive field centers and measures population averages, while single cells show scatter (~7° in V1) around the local mean.
evaluation: Claims C190-C198 provide a thoughtful analysis of methodological differences affecting coverage estimates. The comparison to prior single-cell data (C191, cited to Wagor et al. 1980) is appropriate. The explanations based on receptive field size (C193-C195) and population averaging (C196-C198) are well-reasoned, with the scatter estimate (C198) appropriately cited to Bonin et al. 2011.

result: No higher visual areas (even those immediately surrounding V1) contain a complete description of the visual hemifield, meaning information on features subtending more than approximately a quarter of the visual field will be routed to different early visual areas with different functional properties.
evaluation: Claims C199-C200 draw an important functional inference from the coverage analysis. Even allowing for underestimation (C190), the complementary rather than redundant coverage patterns (C6, C189) support this conclusion. This has implications for understanding visual processing in mice, though the functional consequences remain to be tested experimentally.

result: GCaMP6 fluorescence is established as a tool for generating retinotopic maps of mouse cortex, with superior signal-to-noise ratio enabling rapid mapping and revelation of new field sign patches (MMA, MMP, RLL, RS), bringing the total to 16 distinct retinotopically-organized regions in mouse cortex.
evaluation: Claims C8, C201-C204 summarize the major methodological and empirical contributions. The establishment of GCaMP6 as a mapping tool (C201) is well-supported by the comprehensive characterization. The superior SNR (C202) enabled discovery of new patches (C203), and the total count of 16 regions (C8, C204) is clearly enumerated (12 published + 4 new).

result: Area P extends across the posterior extent of V1, consistent with prior tracer studies and recent functional maps, though signal-to-noise may be limited in this posterior region near the cranial window edge, and additional retinotopic structure may exist under the transverse sinus or in folded cortex.
evaluation: Claims C205-C210 discuss the posterior extent of the maps with appropriate caveats. The extension of P (C205) is supported by prior anatomical (C206) and functional (C207) work. The acknowledgment of potential limitations (C208-C210) is appropriate scientific caution, though these remain speculative (C210).

result: Two field sign patches (MMA and MMP) were identified in the MM region between AM/PM and retrosplenial cortex, consistent with prior anatomical evidence for multiple distinct regions in MM and direct V1 projections terminating in distinct anterior and posterior regions.
evaluation: Claims C211-C214 connect the functional findings to prior anatomical work. The identification of MMA and MMP (C211) is well-supported by the mapping data. The consistency with prior anatomical observations (C212-C213, cited to Van der Gucht et al. 2007 and Wang and Burkhalter 2007) and the inference about correspondence (C214) strengthen the interpretation.

result: RLL is biased toward the nasal, lower visual field (like RL) and may convey visual information on whisker location to barrel cortex, while the visual map in retrosplenial cortex is consistent with its visual responsiveness and role in spatial memory and navigation.
evaluation: Claims C216-C219 make functional speculations about the newly identified patches. While the visual field bias of RLL (C216) is supported by data, the proposed function (C217) is speculative. The consistency with retrosplenial cortex function (C218-C219) is reasonable but requires experimental validation. These are plausible hypotheses for future work rather than demonstrated results.

result: While some areas might be activated more effectively by stimuli other than checkerboards, the broad spatial and temporal frequency content of checkerboard borders, combined with retinotopic regions occupying most territory between primary sensory areas, suggests few additional visual areas remain to be discovered and substantial differences with different stimuli would not be expected.
evaluation: Claims C220-C226 address potential limitations of the stimulus choice. The acknowledgment that different stimuli might activate some areas differently (C220-C222) is appropriate, but the argument that checkerboards contain broad frequency content (C223) and that most territory is already mapped (C224) provides reasonable justification for the conclusions (C225-C226).

result: Population imaging naturally limits resolution, and widefield fluorescence includes signals from dendrites and axons that may cross borders, yet widefield and 2-photon border locations differ by only tens of micrometers, suggesting border blurring is minimal despite these potential confounds.
evaluation: Claims C227-C233 provide a thoughtful discussion of methodological limitations. The acknowledgment of potential resolution limits (C227-C229) and border-crossing processes (C230-C232) is appropriate. The close agreement between widefield and 2-photon borders (C233, 30 μm difference from C172) provides empirical evidence that these concerns do not substantially affect the results.

result: The cellular and laminar origins of widefield GCaMP6 fluorescence remain unknown, and some observed retinotopic organization (e.g., in retrosplenial and barrel cortices) may result from retinotopically-organized axons rather than somatic retinotopy, as suggested by the lack of retinotopy in these regions in Rorb-Ai93 mice (which label layer 4/5 somata).
evaluation: Claims C234-C236, C90-C91 acknowledge an important limitation and provide evidence bearing on it. The lack of retinotopy in retrosplenial/barrel cortex in Rorb-Ai93 mice (C236) suggests these signals may arise from axons rather than local somata, supporting the use of 'patch' rather than 'area' terminology (C91, C237-C242). This is an appropriate interpretation of the data.

result: In prior architectonic-based maps, V1, AL, LM, and RL borders intersect at a common point, but retinotopic maps show the V1 border is more medial, such that V1 and AL lack a common border, with RL and LM sharing a ~100-300 μm border between them, and the architectonic V1 border running through RL and LM to intersect AL's medial tip.
evaluation: Claims C243-C249 explain how the border mismatch reconciles differences between prior maps. The comparison to prior architectonic maps (C243, cited to Wang and Burkhalter 2007) is appropriate. The spatial relationships described (C244-C248) follow logically from the border mismatch findings, and the interpretation that this helps explain map differences (C249) is reasonable.

result: The consistent mismatch between architectonic and retinotopic V1 borders across three methods indicates the architectonic border may correlate with functions other than retinotopic reversal, possibly including the binocular region (as RL and LM include binocular zone representations) or a thin monocular zone along the medial edge of LM and RL.
evaluation: Claims C250-C254 provide plausible hypotheses for the functional significance of the border mismatch. The consistency across methods (C250) supports that this is a real phenomenon. The proposed explanations involving binocular representation (C252-C253, cited to Wagor et al. 1980) or a monocular zone (C254, cited to Laing et al. 2015) are reasonable hypotheses that warrant future investigation.
